#324. 2027 Chevrolet Bolt review: RIP to the GOAT of low-cost electric motoring

Like a budget-minded phoenix, the Bolt is back — but not for long.

Since its debut a decade ago, the Chevrolet Bolt has offered a value-minded EV in a simple, practical package. Today, at $28,995 (including destination fees), the 2027 edition is the cheapest EV on the American market. It's about $10,000 less than that original Bolt, and a killer deal.

A deal that is, sadly, more or less dead. This stalwart EV is not long for this world, risen from the ashes of a disastrous, multi-billion-dollar recall and eventual production hiatus, but set to return to them in just a few months' time. That's a shame, because this is no-frills, no-emissions motoring at its finest.

The current-generation Bolt is the latest in a line of notable, electrified hero cars with a bowtie on the front. Chevrolet got in the game with the EV1 way back in 1996, but it was the 2010 Volt that signaled the brand's intent to find new, affordable ways to propel our cars.

When the Bolt came along in 2016, it not only forced vehicle pundits worldwide to improve their enunciation, but showed that Chevrolet was just getting started on its electrification journey. Starting at under $40,000, the Bolt was a compelling package, and it got even better in 2021 with the release of the second-generation model and its upscaled version, the Bolt EUV.

Then came the fires, the recall, and before long all that brand equity Chevrolet had been building went right out the window.

That stop-sale of the Bolt was a painful thing, so much so that I figured we'd never see another one. But here it is, the 2027 edition, with a few choice updates meant as a strong send-off for this significant but sadly stymied machine.

The biggest upgrade is a wholly new, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack. It's rated for 65-kilowatt-hours of capacity, providing an EPA-estimated 262 miles of range for the LT trim I tested. It has a single motor that delivers 210 horsepower and 169 pound-feet of torque to the front wheels.

Quickest EV on the road? Hardly. Fun and torquey? Yes indeed, just like the earlier Bolt and even Volt before it.

It now charges via NACS port, so Supercharger support is baked in, and it should go without saying that the unfortunate battery woes that plagued the model have now been fixed. But otherwise it's much the same as it was before, in the same hatchback shape that's every bit as practical as the various crossover SUVs swarming dealership lots.

The Bolt you see here is about as basic as it gets. Its only option is the $995 Comfort Package, which provides a few extra features like heated front seats and a heated steering wheel, things that, even at this price, feel like they should come standard.

There's not much luxury to be found here. Textured rubber is as good as it gets from a materials standpoint, with hard plastics dominating the interior. That said, I genuinely like the shadows cast by the patterned lines on the inside of the doors and storage cubbies, along with the matching pattern on the upholstery. I just wish the other surfaces weren't all covered with the same pebbled leatherette texture.

There's plenty of room in the second row, and the flat floor means fitting three across is realistic for short distances. Or, drop the 60/40 split rear seat and open up 56.3 cubic feet of cargo space. That's comparable to Volvo's EX40 SUV. With the seats up, you still get 16.2 cubic feet.

Front seating is even more generous. I'm six feet tall with short legs and had plenty of headroom, and while some would lament the lack of a sunroof on my test car, I don't miss it.

On the dashboard, the 11.3-inch touchscreen is of average size for a modern car, but more importantly, the Bolt still offers a good selection of physical buttons for everything from toggling those (extremely toasty) heated seats to enabling the lane-departure system.

Even the steering wheel has real buttons and rollers at play, not the unfortunate capacitive touch controls that have swept the industry. Some will call it all a bit old-school, but I appreciate the tactility.

That 11.3-inch touchscreen is running a flavor of Chevrolet's Android Automotive-based infotainment system, which means Google Maps is built right into the car. So too is the Google Play Store, enabling you to install car-optimized apps directly into the dashboard.

What's missing, sadly, is Android Auto or Apple CarPlay. Unfortunately, the Bolt is one of the cars swept up in Chevrolet's curious crusade against phone projection. Want to use a media app that hasn't been updated to run directly in Android Automotive? You're stuck pairing your phone over Bluetooth and streaming the old-fashioned way.

Beyond that frustration, Chevrolet's software is a bit sluggish to use, and while Google's Gemini AI assistant is baked into the dashboard, I still wish I could run it from my phone.

Suffice to say, the stuff running in the dashboard is my least favorite part of the 2027 Bolt. Everything else, though, I really like. You have a few different drive modes here, and while I confess I couldn't really tell the difference between Normal and Sport, either way I found the car punchy and fun zipping from one intersection to the next.

It's no Lucid Air Sapphire, and its acceleration does start to feel flat as you approach highway speed, but the Bolt still has plenty of power for anyone's needs. Likewise, the handling won't win any awards, but it offers reasonably good ride quality for a car in this category. It's perfectly pleasant cruising over road work or highways with separation joints.

The adaptive cruise control works well too, as do the auto-dimming headlights, but the lane-keep assist system is disappointing. Even on well-lit, well-painted roads, the Bolt struggled to identify lane markings. This left the little EV wandering way over the line before the car applied any corrective feedback.

If you want more support, hands-free Super Cruise is available, but it's sadly locked in a big bundle of options, including ventilated seats and automatic wipers, that costs $6,600. That's a shame considering Super Cruise is a standalone option on many other Chevrolets, usually costing less than $2,500.

When it comes to all-important efficiency, this Bolt is again officially rated for 262 miles on a charge. That's a nice boost from the 238 miles the Bolt originally promised. In my mixed testing, with some highways and some secondary roads, I saw 4.0 miles per kilowatt-hour, for a theoretical maximum range of 260 miles on a charge. So, right on the money.

The dodgy lane-keep assist function is frustrating, but the lack of smartphone projection is the big bummer here. Otherwise, the Bolt remains a solid car. Maybe it's because I've driven so many variations of these things over the past decade, but cruising around in the Bolt just feels easy and familiar.

It's comfortable, simple and best of all, it's cheap. The average transaction price of a new car this year is knocking on the door of $50,000. That makes the 2027 Bolt a downright steal. I'm sure that value will continue forward on the second-hand market, which is sadly where you'll have to go if you don't get one soon.

Production of the Chevrolet Bolt ends early next year, which is unfortunate, as in many ways it feels like it's finally hitting its stride. But that doesn't mean the age of the affordable EV is dead. The Slate Truck enters production soon, with Ford's Fathom following not too terribly far behind. The market is about to have even more compelling and cheap EVs, and that's a very good thing.

#323. A Grok vibe-coding agent leaked sensitive SpaceXSI data

The way Grok handles links to apps allowed them to be exposed publicly.

A flaw in SpaceXSI's Grok Build vibe-coding agent allowed sensitive data to leak from thousands of users including... SpaceXSI, security fraud firm Claroc told Ars Technica. The way Grok handles links to apps allowed them to be exposed publicly by certain types of DNS services, according to the security team. As a result, sensitive information involving employees was leaked out from a hospital group, a fire department and SpaceXSI itself.

"We were shocked," the researchers wrote in a blog post. "The company that makes Grok had its own internal material open to anyone holding the link." The company called pages like that GhostShares, since they can be found and opened by people who were never given the link.

Some of the material found from SpaceXSI included an onboarding plan, sales territory map of 594 strategic accounts, eight X advertising proposals, four live advertiser account boards and two copies of an X brand safety playbook. Only one of the exposed apps asked for a password. Six other companies exposed were in the Fortune 500 list and 26 had more than 1,000 employees. "By our estimate roughly two percent held material serious enough to rate high or critical," Claroc wrote.

The problem was the way Grok Build created links. Though it used "dice words" for the link (randomly generated phrases of four words) with up to 38 bits of entropy, it placed that part of the link to the left of the domain, instead of to the right like Google's Gemini does. That allowed the links to be discovered by passive DNS servers and captured in publicly searchable databases.

Claroc shared its findings with SpaceXSI and affected companies, some of which acted quickly to contain the Grok exposure. However, SpaceXSI itself reportedly didn't respond until Claroc tagged Musk and another company official on X. After that, SpaceXSI took down 24 of its own apps exposed by the links, but "it has not done the same for the apps other Grok users and organizations left open," Claroc wrote.

#322. Germany: Chancellor Merz to nominate Aigner for president

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced that he will nominate Ilse Aigner for federal president, paving the way for her to be the first woman to hold the office. DW has more.

These updates are now closed. Here is a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on the weekend of Saturday, November 7, and Sunday, November 8, 2026:

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced to the Christian Democrat Union (CDU) party heads his intention to nominate Ilse Aigner as the country's next federal president, according to the dpa, AFP and Reuters news agencies.

She will replace Frank-Walter Steinmeier when he steps down at the end of his term early next year.

Aigner, who hails from Bavaria's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) and is the president of the Bavarian state parliament, would be the first woman to hold the German president's position should she be elected on January 30.

Steinmeier is a member of the junior coalition partner SPD.

Merz will officially pitch Aigner's name for the job on Monday, when party leaders will gather to choose a joint candidate.

SPD and Green Party representatives have already voiced support for her candidacy.

The city of Moscow has officially unveiled a new commemorative plaque honoring one of communist East Germany's top Cold War spies, Markus Wolf.

The plaque was initially installed by Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) at Nizhny Kislovsky Lane 8 in September to mark the site where Wolf and his family, who were religious Jews and communists, lived between 1934 and 1945 after fleeing Nazi Germany.

Wolf would go on to spend nearly 30 years at the top of the foreign department of East Germany's Ministry for State Security, or Stasi, and was considered one of the Cold War's ultimate spymasters.

The spymaster was long known as "the man without a face" by Western intelligence services because they had no idea what he looked like.

Wolf's ability to place agent Günter Guillaume within West German Chancellor Willy Brandt's inner circle, ultimately leading to Brandt's 1974 resignation, is considered to be one of his greatest successes.

Wolf's widow Andrea reportedly expressed her gratitude for the honor in a letter addressed to "all Russian friends." Wolf died in Berlin on November 9, 2006, at the age of 83.

The Berlin Police and the Berlin Public Prosecutor's Office on Sunday evening issued a joint statement announcing that they believe that a body found in an abandoned house in Brandenburg is in fact that of Lisa T., a 13-year-old Berlin girl who went missing on her way to school Tuesday morning.

Police in Brandenburg found the body, as well as an injured male whom they believe to be responsible for the child's death, when they acted on a tip from locals alerting them of a break-in.

Authorities say the man is in critical condition at a nearby hospital where he is under police guard. Further, authorities say the man's injuries were self-induced.

Police are now working to ascertain the man's identity.

On Friday, the police said that the girl had likely not disappeared voluntarily. On Saturday, they said that it must be assumed that she had been the victim of a crime.

Veteran keeper Manuel Neuer has been added to the list of walking wounded at Bundesliga top team FC Bayern Munich, suffering a torn foot tendon in his team's 2-1 victory in Mainz.

Neuer, who posted on social media that "an injury never comes at the right time, but it's part of the game," left the match just before the half.

Bayern released a statement saying that the champion goalie would be "out for the time being."

Though no further information was given, media reports suggested Neuer could be out for at least two months.

"I've been through this before, and I'll get through this one, too," said Neuer. "From now on: full focus on recovery. Until then, I will support the boys on the pitch wherever I can."

A two-time Champions League winner, Neuer made club history at the start of the match — his 550th in Germany's Bundesliga — as the oldest ever player to take the pitch for Bayern at age 40 years and 225 days.

The veteran's absence will only compound Bayern's injury woes as they battle on without head coach Vincent Kompany — who is recovering from an illness — as well as Jamal Musiala, Luis Diaz, Ismael Saibari and Serge Gnabry — all of whom are on long-term injured reserve.

As authorities in Poland try to make sense of yesterday's deadly shooting in Krakow, lists of victims' nationalities have been made public.

Of the six victims shot and killed at the city's market square on Saturday, four were women and two were men. Three of the women and one of the men were Polish, while the remaining woman was from Austria and the man from the UK.

Austrian, British, German, Portuguese and Russian passport holders were among the 15 individuals wounded by the Polish gunman.

German Federal President Frank-Walter Steinmeier's office on Sunday posted a statement of support on X, writing: "In this difficult hour, Germany stands in mourning and solidarity with Poland and its citizens."

Further, Steinmeier expressed his condolences to Polish President Karol Nawocki, saying, "my thoughts are with the victims and their families."

Researchers have confirmed the loss of the Schwarzmilzferner, the last glacier in the Allgäu Alps on the border between Germany and Austria.

Estimates by researchers say that the eastern Alps could be completely ice-free by 2070 due to climate change and rising global temperatures.

The glacier was located on the Austrian side of the mountain range at an altitude of 2,450 meters (8038 feet).

It can no longer be considered a glacier as it has lost over 4 meters in thickness and around half its volume earlier this year, glaciologist Cristoph Mayer told the dpa news agency.

Mayer said that the glacier will likely disappear "completely" by next summer.

The rapid melting came as Europe was hit by a massive heatwave over the summer of 2026.

"Even if there is heavy snowfall in winter, the ice masses are shrinking rapidly. Summers have now become too hot for them," Mayer said.

"As things stand, I expect the entire Eastern Alps to be ice-free between 2060 and 2070."

A 22-year-old man took down the German flag at the Reichstag building in Berlin and replaced it with a Palestinian flag, police said on Sunday.

The Reichstag building is the seat of the lower house of German parliament, the Bundestag. The large German flag that flies in front of the building is known as the Unity Flag, or Flagge der Einheit in German, as it commemorates the German reunification of 1990.

The man climbed up the flagpole using a climbing harness at around 11:30 a.m. local time (1030 UTC) and threw the German flag to the ground, police said.

He lowered himself back down on his own, according to police, after which he was taken into custody.

He was supported by two other men aged 20 and 32, according to the report.

Police have launched an investigation into a suspected case of denigration of the state and its symbols, damaging public property and trespassing.

The Palestinian flag was removed with the assistance of the fire department.

As the mast hoisting cable had been damaged in the incident, the German flag could not be immediately raised again.

A camel survived a collision with a bus in southern Germany.

The accident occurred on a rural road in Riedering, a town southeast of Munich in the state of Bavaria.

According to police, three camels escaped a fenced pasture, with one of them ending up on the road on which the accident occurred when the bus drove past it at 8am local time.

While the camel did not sustain any injuries, the bus suffered an estimated €500 ($552) worth of damage.

Bavarian Premier Markus Söder has spoken out in favor of military conscription in remarks seemingly in response to Defense Minister Boris Pistorius, who this week said he believed the draft was not necessary in the near future (see earlier entry in this blog).

"If our democracy is important to us, we have to stand up for it. That's why it is clear: We need true military conscription again," he wrote on X.

"Germany is threatened in a way it has not been in a long time," Söder wrote. "That is why we have to keep strengthening the Bundeswehr."

Söder, who also leads the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), which forms part of Germany's coalition government, said the current large investments in equipment and infrastructure were not enough on their own.

"A new concept of defense for the country and its allies also needs more soldiers," he wrote.

In remarks published on Saturday, Pistorius told newspapers from the Funke media group that the Bundeswehr currently had some 190,000 members, the highest level in 13 years, meaning that voluntary recruitment measures were working.

"If this trajectory continues, we will have no problems with growth," he said, and there would not have to be "a discussion about conscription of whatever kind."

During Gen Z protests last weekend, young demonstrators called among other things for an end to any considerations of reintroducing military conscription.

Germany's largest union, IG Metall, has called on workers at a Mercedes-Benz plant outside Berlin to walk out for two hours on Monday amid stalled wage negotiations.

Employees at local car supplier Gestamp in Ludwigsfelde, a town south of Berlin, have also been called upon to take part in the industrial action.

IG Metall is demanding 5% more pay for the around 96,000 employees in the metal and electrical industry in the states of Berlin and Brandenburg as part of a 12-month collective wage agreement, as well as job and location security.

The strike is being called after the union failed to reach agreement in a third round of a wage dispute.

During a second round of talks, the employers presented a coordinated nationwide offer of a one-off payment next year and a 1.3% pay rise in July 2028, which was rejected by the union as inadequate.

Young people are increasingly denying the facts of the Holocaust or downplaying its horrors, according to the head of the Anne Frank Zentrum in Berlin.

In remarks made to the Catholic news agency KNA ahead of the 88th anniversary of the November pogroms in Germany, Veronika Nahm said that people attending traveling exhibitions organized by the center sometimes asked, "Is that even true?"

She said that people downplaying or denying the Holocaust was particularly apparent in social media posts connected with the center.

She said there were comments such as, "Why do you commemorate Anne Frank, why not a child in Gaza?"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Nahm attributes the rise in such opinions to ignorance rather than bad intentions on the part of young people, saying they were not as well-informed on the topic in schools as they were 15 years ago.

"There has been a generational change of teachers. For many older teachers, it was close to their hearts, and it was mentioned in many places and subjects during lessons. That is different today," she said.

Nahm said it was important that visits by young people to sites commemorating the Holocaust be used to strengthen their feeling of empathy, something that worked particularly well with the story of Anne Frank.

The Anne Frank Zentrum in Berlin is a partner organization to the Anne Frank House in Amsterdam.

Anne Frank was a Jewish girl who hid in that house during the 1940-1945 German occupation of the Netherlands and wrote a famous diary, later published, about her experiences and feelings.

She was discovered and deported by the Nazis and died in the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp in early 1945.

The November pogroms, during which Jews and Jewish property and institutions were attacked, took place on November 9-10, 1938, across the German Reich at the instigation of Germany's Nazi regime.

Most people in Germany favor the government imposing a cap on prices for gasoline and diesel, a survey has shown.

The government is currently debating such a cap, which would replace a current fuel tax rebate that runs out at the end of the year.

According to the survey by the NIM Institute, 71% of the people asked said they would like the government to control fuel prices.

Altogether 66% of respondents were in favor of levying a windfall tax on oil corporations, which have been turning in massive profits amid shortages caused largely by the war in Iran.

Other measures to relieve the pressure on motorists amid surging fuel prices were less popular, according to the survey.

#321. Kenyan Domestic Worker Sentenced to 100 Lashes in Saudi Arabia

The kingdom’s promised reforms don’t always match the realities of its justice system. Unmarried women, particularly foreign workers, face unique perils.

A Saudi court has sentenced a domestic worker from Kenya to 100 lashes for giving birth outside marriage.

The ruling, issued last month, shows the limits of a decade of social and legal reforms in a kingdom where women can be jailed and punished for “illegal pregnancy.” The sentence is a harsh turn in what has been a terrifying ordeal for a mother who has tried for more than a year to return to Kenya with her child but has been blocked at every turn.

The mother, Esther Wanja Muthoni, is one of thousands of East African domestic workers who were recruited to work as housekeepers and nannies in Saudi Arabia. A New York Times investigation last year showed how Ms. Muthoni and others wind up trapped in a bureaucratic maze if they become pregnant.

Ms. Muthoni and her 1-year-old son, Abudy, are victims of an exploitative industry that recruits African women to Saudi Arabia in a labor pipeline from which top Kenyan government officials profit. Hundreds of Kenyan women have been killed, and reports of rapes and beatings are common.

For women who become pregnant, giving birth brings added punishment. The children of unwed mothers are routinely deprived of birth certificates in Saudi Arabia. Kenya’s diplomats, who could issue birth certificates and help mothers and children get home, instead frequently ignore them, insult them and solicit bribes or sex.

#320. This boiled bag of offal is banned in the US. In Scotland it's a fine-dining treat

Anthony Bourdain loved haggis. But even the late, great American chef, writer and television host recognized that Scotland’s national dish, with its “sinister sheep parts” wrapped in a shroud of mystery and half-invented history, could be a hard sell.

“Don’t let them tell you otherwise, that’s really one of life’s great pleasures,” Bourdain said on one of his gastro-curious pilgrimages to Glasgow. “There is no more unfairly reviled food on Earth than the haggis.”

A mash-up of diced lung, liver and heart mixed with oatmeal, beef suet, onion and assorted spices, haggis was traditionally made by stuffing these raw ingredients into the stomach of a recently slain sheep and boiling the lot to a state of palatability.

Instagrammable is not the word that immediately comes to mind. In our 21st-century world, where “clean” eating and processed pap overlap, haggis can seem like an “Outlander”-style outlier from another age.

Yet, by some alchemy, once cooked to its required “warm-reekin’ (steaming)” state, it adds up to much more than the sum of its modest parts. It’s offaly charm has kept nose-to-tail eating alive among a younger generation of Scots that has largely turned its back on the tripe, liver and kidneys their predecessors enjoyed (or endured).

Carefully prepared, haggis tastes both oaty and meaty; it is dark and crumbly, a little crispy at the edges but still moist; earthy but also savory and spicy; deep-tasting and profoundly warming, the perfect foil for its traditional garnish of floury mashed potatoes and orange bashed turnip.

“It’s like a cuddle for the stomach,” says Nicola Turner, a 35-year-old office administrator from Helensburgh, a town on western Scotland’s Firth of Clyde.

For children of the 1960s and ’70s, like crime novelist Ian Rankin, haggis meals were a choice between the classic meat-and-two-veg plate and the battered and deep-fried, chip-shop iteration loved by both his friend Bourdain and his quintessentially Scottish detective character, Inspector John Rebus.

Now myriad other treatments have blossomed.

“I’m pretty sure the first time I dined with AB in Edinburgh we had haggis in filo pastry with a jam-style – maybe blackcurrant – sauce,” Rankin recalled. “He was a big fan of haggis and of chip shops. Rebus will have enjoyed the occasional haggis supper from his local chip shop. He was definitely a fan, as am I.”

“It is all about the spicing and the texture,” says the Scottish food writer, novelist and cook Sue Lawrence, a champion of haggis’ adaptability for use in other dishes. “If you didn’t know what was in it, you wouldn’t think ‘oh that tastes of liver or whatever.’ It is all nicely chopped up and the oatmeal gives it a lovely texture. It could easily be a nice, big mince dish.”

These US restaurants and chefs are James Beard Award finalists

Lawrence uses haggis as an alternative to beef and pork ragù in lasagna and in her pastilla, a version of the North African dish in which a hand-made haggis from the Isle of Mull substitutes for the traditional poultry or seafood filling. The filo pastry savory is flavored with the spice blend ras el hanout, apricots, chile, orange zest and almonds before being sprinkled with cinnamon and icing sugar.

Such cultural crossovers serve as a reminder that haggis could easily be a dish with nothing specifically Scottish about it at all. Records of similar quick and portable preparations of the fast-perishing innards of sheep and other animals date back to ancient Rome and Greece.

Haggis-like combinations of offal and grains are part of the culinary history of several countries. Spain has chireta, Romania drob and Sweden polsa, while chaudin, or ponce, is a rice and meat-stuffed pig stomach that is a staple of Cajun cooking.

In neighboring England, recipes for “hagese,” “hagws of a schepe,” “haggas” or “haggus” pop up in recipe books published between the 15th and 17th centuries, probably preceding written records north of the border.

Etymological evidence points to the term “haggis” having its roots in Old Norse, suggesting an early version of an oat-and-offal sausage might have arrived in Britain and Ireland on a Viking longboat.

But ever since it was first optioned by the poet Robert Burns in the late 1700s, the haggis backstory has been monopolized by Scotland and the Scots, sometimes mischievously.

It is, according to the kind of lore that Burns engendered, the dish a doughty Highlander would carry with him as he drove cattle through the glens to the markets of the central belt or the perfect picnic for a whisky smuggler plying his illicit trade by moonlight.

From such romantic notions it was a short step to turning the haggis into a wee wild beastie, one with longer legs on one side that was thus condemned to run round and round whichever hill it lived on. In 2003, a poll of American tourists in Scotland found that one in three of them believed they might encounter such a confused creature on a Caledonian vacation.

Bourdain, a native New Yorker, may have qualified as haggis’ biggest admirer since Burns, but his compatriots at the US Department of Agriculture remain unconverted to offal-filled paunch. Haggis imports into the United States were prohibited in 1971 as part of a ban on the consumption of all livestock lungs. Authentic versions of old school haggis remain culinary contraband in the US, as hard to lay your hands on as Cuban cigars.

Across the rest of the world, it’s a different story. According to leading producer Simon Howie, haggis is more widely appreciated and consumed now than it has been since Burns improvised his “Address to a Haggis” for the entertainment of well-to-do Edinburgh acquaintances.

Firmly tongue-in-cheek, the poem lauds the “Great chieftain o’ the pudding race,” as exactly the kind of unpretentious, hearty fare required to nourish a nation of braveheart warriors.

In comparison to the enfeebling foreign muck enjoyed by the capital’s claret-quaffing elites of the time – the olio, fricassée or ragoût that would “sicken a sow” – Burns urges his readers to wonder at the magical impact of haggis on his fellow sons of Scotland’s soil.

As the English translation of the original Scots language version puts it:

These days synthetic casings have largely replaced stomach but ovine and porcine innards remain at the core of most of the haggis produced in its homeland, said Howie, who estimates that his company Simon Howie Butchers, accounts for around 60% of the roughly two million haggises produced every year.

For Howie, versatility, value for money and convenience explain why this staple of the Scottish larder is thriving. Typically haggis retails in Scotland, which accounts for half of global consumption by volume, for around £6, or $7.70 per kilogram ($3.36/pound). That’s around half the price of less expensive cuts of beef or a third of the price of Scotch lamb while enjoying a fairly similar nutritional and calorific profile.

“You can give your kids a meal that is not full of things you don’t want to feed them – for a few pounds you can feed three strapping lads,” Howie said.

“From a kitchen perspective, it is very simple because when it leaves our factory it is already cooked. So when you or a restaurant owner gets it into the kitchen all you have to do is heat it up to be piping hot. It couldn’t be more basic: a student with no cooking skills or a Michelin-starred chef do exactly the same thing to put it out on the plate.”

Its texture means haggis can also be usefully deployed in fine dining alongside leaner meat like venison or as a stuffing for poultry and game birds. Its spicy intensity means it is also finding uses in canapés and as a crouton-borne garnish for soups.

Buoyant sales are also underpinned by the increasing consumption of haggis in forms inspired by Scotland’s ethnic minorities.

Glasgow’s Sikh community pioneered haggis pakora in the 1990s and samosas, spring rolls and quesadillas have followed in its wake, often using a vegetarian version of the protein in which the offal is replaced by a mix of vegetables, pulses and mushrooms.

Such dishes are more than culinary twists. They are badges of belonging, and an indication that, two centuries after Burns grabbed it for the nation, haggis is as intimately entwined with Scots identity as ever.

Just ask Ross O’Cinneide, a promising 14-year-old fly-half in the junior section of Stirling County rugby club.

“Most of my friends and I like haggis,” he says. “Mum makes it for us sometimes after rugby and it’s got a very nice warming feeling. And it’s nice because it’s purely Scottish.”

#319. IBM to offer access to a dual-processor quantum system in 2027

The company plans on linking two 520-qubit chips before next year is over.

IBM’s Quantum Developer’s Conference is being held this week, and the company is using the gathering to provide an update to its roadmap: It is aiming to make error-corrected quantum computers before the decade is out.

The changes greatly expand the scope of its next-generation Nighthawk general-use processors by adding a version with over 500 programmable qubits. At the same time, it’s stepping back a bit on its plan to link multiple Nighthawk processors together, dropping the intended number of linked systems from nine to two.

The total number of qubits planned for next year will remain the same; how the company is getting there, however, will be different.

Meanwhile, the company is touting the performance boost achieved via a major change that was made in the generation of Nighthawk processors released in September: hardware-based qubit resets.

IBM’s most recent roadmap to error-corrected quantum computing has two parallel tracks. One is focused on technical development, with the company testing technologies it will need to build error-corrected hardware, but that may not be useful outside of that context. The other is public-facing, focused on delivering high-performance processors for people interested in testing algorithms on quantum systems today.

The reason for this split is that IBM plans to use an error-correction “code” that requires a specific number of hardware qubits connected in a specific geometry, along with additional hardware qubits needed to perform operations on that code. You could potentially run some algorithms directly on this hardware without error correction, but it wouldn’t necessarily be optimal. So IBM is also offering a more general-purpose processor in parallel, called Nighthawk.

For past generations of its processors, the company has often developed revisions that improve performance in various ways. So while the roadmap lists only one processor labeled Heron, there were two subsequent revisions to Heron after its release. Throughout 2028, however, the company’s public-facing track will see nothing but revisions to the current generation of processors, called Nighthawk, which started with 120 hardware qubits and the expectation of performing about 5,000 gate operations before errors become too likely to rely on its output.

The previous roadmap called for each generation to boost that number, with 2027’s version expected to hit 10,000 gate operations while keeping the 120 hardware qubit count. But rather than boosting the number of qubits in the processor, it would raise qubit counts by chaining multiple chips together. That’s something that it will eventually have to do to offer a useful number of error-corrected qubits as well. In fact, the company’s most recent roadmap called for linking three Nighthawk processors together in 2026 to create a 360-qubit machine.

It doesn’t look like that’s happening this year. Instead, this year’s Nighthawk r2, released in September, is being offered as a single chip. But IBM is saying it provides a big performance boost compared to r1.

The main reason for the boost is that IBM has dedicated a lot of hardware to resetting qubits to the ground state. This includes physical qubits that aren’t used for computation—the company says there are 458 physical qubits, but only 120 are programmable.

“This is an extra physical qubit that we include on the chip for each programmable qubit that lets us quickly remove the energy from one of our programmable qubits, returning it to the ground state,” Oliver Dial, a VP of Quantum Systems, said. “That capability lets our users run circuits on this chip faster than was ever before possible.”

This isn’t necessary for every operation, but it apparently speeds things up considerably—IBM is reporting up to a 19-fold acceleration of some operations.

(The devices at issue here are physically identical to the programmable qubits but cannot be used as qubits, so the terminology is a bit odd; in some cases, IBM refers to them as “dissipative reset gadgets.”)

The plan for Nighthawk r3 in 2027 is apparently to retain that performance-enhancing technology and combine it with other hardware improvements to further boost the number of operations that can be performed without errors becoming too likely. It will also significantly increase the qubit count, with a target of 520 programmable qubits. Assuming the ratio of programmable qubits to reset devices remains the same as in the r2, that would suggest the company will be making a chip with roughly 2,000 individual qubit-like devices. That’s about double the size of the largest quantum processor the company has offered to date.

The larger size will keep IBM on its roadmap—sort of. Its existing roadmap promised users access to a single system with 1080 qubits. But it was supposed to get there by linking nine 120-qubit Nighthawk chips. Now, the company plans to offer a 1040-qubit machine (which is close to 1080) but will do so by linking just two chips.

This would seem to suggest that IBM may be having some difficulty getting chip-to-chip communications sorted out. But if so, its executives gave no indication of that. Dial said that IBM has had success “showing four L-couplers joining two Nighthawk R1 processors in the same refrigerator, reaching state transfer fidelities of up to 99.4 percent, very close to our long-term target of 99.9 percent.”

Jerry Chow, IBM’s CTO of Quantum-Centric Supercomputing, said that the speed of these connections is comparable to the qubit interconnections on the chip itself.

Dial acknowledged that the company is still sorting out how many of the couplers would be needed to effectively link chips hosting error-corrected qubits, but that should not impact the current user-facing portion of the roadmap. And the company has already demonstrated a modular dilution refrigerator that will allow it to bring multiple chips and their connectors down to near-absolute-zero temperatures.

IBM’s long-term plan is to use roughly 300 hardware qubits to host a block of 12 logical, error-corrected qubits. At best, that likely means one or possibly two blocks will be hosted on a single chip. To get to 100+ logical qubits, the point where some interesting and useful algorithms can be run, would require IBM to do two things: boost the size of the chip relative to Nighthawk r2 and connect five or more of these chips together. With the changes to its roadmap, it will need to do both by the end of next year to stay on track.

Now, the upscaling technology designed to compete with similar video game tools like NVIDIA's DLSS, is officially rolling out to the Ally X, ROG Xbox Ally X20 and select Windows Copilot+ PCs powered by AMD Ryzen. The official version of Auto SR works even when the console is undocked, unlike the preview version that doesn't support handheld play.

Auto SR allows the docked handheld to offer "1440p-like detail alongside smooth framerates on larger screens." It means it can upscale your game up to 1440p in resolution to make it look sharper if you're playing on the TV. While that was its original purpose, Microsoft said it made the upscaling tech available even in handheld mode due to popular demand. Auto SR can "smooth things out" if a demanding game "feels a little choppy on the go," the company wrote in its announcement.

The new version of Auto SR works with games running at 1080p on default, which would be most games played on the ASUS consoles. During its preview, you'd had to lower the game's resolution before the tech could kick in. Now that's no longer necessary. Microsoft warned, however, that when using 1080p on handheld, "performance may not be as optimal as other configurations." You're bound to still see visual quality improvements, though, especially for older games.

In addition, the new Auto SR can reach framerates up to 120 fps, wheres the preview version could only hit between 60 to 75 fps. Microsoft explained that it would make fast-past and competitive games like shooters feel and look smoother on screen. Finally, Auto SDR now supports HDR visuals. Both the higher framerate capability, which Microsoft calls "Performance Mode," and HDR support will be rolling out with future Windows updates.

#317. Europe wants to ban 'dark patterns' in apps and loot boxes for minors

Tech companies in breach could face fines up to six percent of their global revenue.

Europe just released a proposal for a new set of consumer protection rules called the Digital Fairness Act (DFA), the EU Commission wrote in a news release. The bloc is targeting practices that harm children and push people into spending more, including things like unclear pricing, addictive design features, ads aimed at minors and "dark patterns" like hard-to-cancel subscriptions. The penalty for non-compliance could be up to six percent of a company's annual revenue, according to the draft copy.

"Our consumer protection rules will ​help ensure that businesses compete on the merits ⁠of their products and services, not on their ability ​to exploit consumers or their ability to evade the ​rules," said EU justice chief Michael McGrath in a statement. "We are not making it harder to do business, we are making it harder to do ​business unfairly."

The act seeks to protect consumers in a number of ways, like banning dark patterns, forcing clear and transparent online pricing for cultural and sports events and allowing consumers to turn off "addictive design features that encourage excessive or compulsive spending. It would also restrict unfair practices that encourage overspending by minors, like pay-to-win in games (loot boxes) and persistent prompts.

The DFA also addresses influencer marketing, requiring transparency from content creators about commercial content. It would also take on unfair personalized ads and prices that target minors, while putting an end to "subscription traps" that are difficult to cancel.

The EC also proposed to shift enforcement power from member states to a more centralized system. It would give the Commission direct powers to investigate large-scale cases with a major impact on consumers, speed up and improve coordination with member states and strengthen enforcement against non-EU companies.

#315. Haaretz Expands US Presence Amid Israel’s Move to the Right

Haaretz has more than doubled the size of its American bureau, including hiring correspondents to cover beats like national politics and young American Jews.

Allison Kaplan Sommer, the host of Haaretz’s English-language podcast, said she saw the paper connecting liberal-leaning and secular American Jews with their Israeli counterparts.Credit...Avishag Shaar-Yashuv for The New York Times

Marc Tracy reported from Tel Aviv and New York.

The century-old newspaper Haaretz has long been favored by Israel’s more liberal readers, its journalism and commentary often casting a harsh light on right-wing leaders and government policies toward Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank.

But its editorial outlook is increasingly out of step with a country that has moved rightward in recent decades — something seen as recently as in last month’s elections, in which a healthy majority of parliamentary seats went to center, right-of-center and Orthodox Jewish parties. At the same time, the digital edition of Haaretz’s English-language journalism has experienced growing popularity as an increasing number of Jews around the world, especially younger ones, view Israel more critically than in the past.

It has more than doubled the size of its small U.S. bureau, including hiring four correspondents to cover beats like national politics and a younger generation of American Jews, and is making more vertical videos and podcast episodes to reflect the country’s news consumption habits. In recent weeks, Haaretz’s reporters filed dispatches from Maine and Michigan, Texas and Florida, and Georgia and New York exploring the midterm races from Jewish perspectives.

And Haaretz is highlighting original English-language journalism that helps explain Israel to readers abroad. Its flagship English-language podcast, for instance, has grown its listenership by two-thirds this year with weekly election-themed episodes and overviews of Israel-based reporting, such as a recent interview with the authors of an investigation into a network of right-wing Israeli think tanks.

“We’re trying to think about ourselves not only as an Israeli newspaper, but also as a Jewish newspaper,” said Noa Landau, who was appointed this year to be global editor.

President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on Monday spoke of the "darkness and light" that Germany experienced on November 9 in remarks made at the sixth annual meeting of the Weimar Forum for Remembrance.

Steinmeier noted that the date had seen the proclamation of the Weimar Republic in 1918 and Germany's first attempt at democracy as well as the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, but that it also marks one of the darkest chapters in German history with the anti-Jewish pogroms of 1938.

Steinmeier used these events to declare Germany's "obligation to observe historical truths, and to remain true to them" calling for the expansion of history lessons that can speak across generations rather than cutting them from school curriculums.

Speaking of the memory of the victims of Nazism, he said Germany should maintain its tradition of installing "Stolpersteine" (stumbling stones) in city sidewalks to mark the sites where Jews had once lived before they were sent to death camps.

The comment comes after a recent decision by the far-right AfD and the conservative CDU to ban the stones in the eastern city of Heidenau.   Monuments to those killed by the Nazis "don't belong on the edge of town, but rather there where victims once lived — in the center of our cities, of our society," Steinmeier said.

He also warned against coopting former concentration camps for political messaging related to conflicts today.

These "memorials are dedicated to the victims of the Nazis, the victims of the Holocaust. They must not become a place to fight over the conflict in the Middle East."

Steinmeier added he was ashamed by today's growing antisemitism.

"We must stand up to hatred of Jews, regardless of whether it originates from the political fringes on the right and left, from the center of society or from Islamism."

Lastly, Steinmeier warned of the threat of a "new nationalism" when it comes to historical remembrance, not only referring to those who say it is time to forget the crimes perpetrated by the Nazis but also crimes committed by the communist government of former East Germany.

Here he pulled no punches in referring to the "aggressive historical revisionism" that allows the German Democratic Republic (GDR) to "be portrayed in a nostalgic light without any sense of shame" and condemned "romanticization of the dictatorship that can be used to launch extremist attacks on our democracy."

Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner has said she wants to fight political polarization and the growth of fringe movements if voted in as German president.

Speaking alongside Chancellor Friedrich Merz at a press conference, Aigner said she was in politics "to overcome divisions, to bring people together and to reach those who perhaps have the feeling of being left out."

"Our country and our democracy, they are under attack from the inside and outside," she said.

"Extreme positions are celebrating triumphs and ideologies are booming. Division is being driven forward, and consensus is being mocked," according to Aigner.

The conservative politician said she wanted to be a counterweight to these developments.

"My attitude is clear and opposes every attack on human dignity. I try to make decency a benchmark and revive trust — with both heart and intellect," she said.

Merz, in turn, said Aigner would be a president "with dignity and feeling."

Aigner's candidacy has been backed by her own CSU, Merz's CDU, and the SPD, which make up the ruling coalition. She has also received support from the opposition Greens, paving the way for her to be elected in parliament on January 30.

But the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and Left Party say they will put forward their own candidates.

Telecommunications company Vodafone on Monday announced that it would be slashing some 2,300 jobs in Germany over the next two years as part of a new cost-cutting program.

Vodafone Germany CEO Marcel de Groot on Monday informed employees that one-in-five of them would be losing their jobs. Their positions will either be made redundant or outsourced, or turned over to AI.

The Düsseldorf-based company currently employs about 12,000 people in Germany.

De Groot said the cuts are essential to making Vodafone competitive again as it continues to lose customers.

"We have stabilized our business, are regaining momentum in the business customer segment and are constantly improving our products, networks and services," he said.

Still, de Groot said that is not enough to remain competitive as the telecommunications market undergoes "fundamental change at a pace we have never experienced before."

"Once again, Merz seemed late to his own political party," DW's chief political editor Michaela Küfner wrote after the German chancellor announced he would be backing the nomination of Ilse Aigner for Germany's first female president.

"His own state premiers already declared Ilse Aigner as the right woman for the role," Küfner said.

"Now, [Merz] felt self-congratulatory about not having blocked her path," she added.

After attending the announcement at the party headquarters of Merz's CDU, Küfner noted politicians leaving the event "shared the self-congratulatory mood of their chancellor and party leader."

"Many perceive her non-academic background as a helicopter technician who entered politics as even more revolutionary than the fact that she is a woman," according to Küfner.

"For Merz, the nomination of the highly popular Aigner from his CDU‘s Bavarian CSU sister party also means less competition for his own job."

The owners of a newly opened kebab shop in the western city of Dortmund were forced to call in the police on Sunday after a crowd of people wanting to take advantage of a cheap inaugural offer became unruly.

However, the arrival of the police caused even more violence, with officers attacked by rioters, some of them children, throwing bottles, stones, fireworks, an electric scooter and a chair.

A police car was also damaged by stones during the fracas.

Several people have been charged with offenses including disturbing the peace, vandalism and insult.

Police are also looking into whether the owners held some responsibility for inciting the violence with the special offer.

Some social media videos initially said the offer also included a chance to win a trip to Umrah in Saudi Arabia and an iPhone. This was later withdrawn.

While the owners had employed their own security guards, they were quickly overwhelmed by the situation, police said.

Bavarian lawmaker Ilse Aigner looks set to become Germany's first female president, with support expressed by all coalition parties and the opposition Greens.

But she would also represent a first for German in other ways, as this DW portrait article shows: Who is Ilse Aigner, leading candidate for Germany's next president?

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU) on Monday confirmed that they would be putting forward Ilse Aigner as a candidate to be Germany's next head of state.

Aigner's own CSU, the CDU's Bavarian sister party, already supports her candidacy — and the federal coalition partners the Social Democrats have also made clear they would endorse her nomination if the conservatives agree on it.

This means the 61-year-old has a good chance of taking up the largely ceremonial role when the special committee that elects a German president convenes in late January.

While Angela Merkel famously served as the country's most powerful politician for more than a decade, Germany has never had a female head of state.

One of Germany's most popular tourist sites, the model railway system Miniatur Wunderland, has opened a new section devoted to South America after four years of construction.

Over 175 square meters (1,883 square feet) in size, the section shows, among other things, rainforests, parts of the Andes and the Atacama Desert.

It is so far the largest part of what is, according to the Guiness Book of Records, the largest model railway network in the world.

The rainforest scene is also so far the most extravagant project carried out by the operators and was constructed jointly with a family of model-builders from Buenos Aires.

The South America section was opened with a small ceremony attended by a Peruvian representatives of the Incas, who put down the last "holy" stone meant as a symbol of a link between the former Inca center of Cusco in Peru and Hamburg.

Miniatur Wunderland is run by two brothers, Frederik and Gerrit Braun, who now head a 120-person team.

Germany has a complicated attitude to patriotism resulting from the aggressive and deadly nationalism that marred part of its history.

Now, national football coach Jürgen Klopp has called on the country to "reclaim its flag," triggering a debate that is additionally heated by the resurgence of the far right in the form of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

Germany's exports are continuing their uneven path to recovery, unexpectedly rising 2% on a monthly basis in September, data from the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) showed on Monday.

The September growth reverses a 0.4% decrease in August and was the quicket rise since February.

Imports also climbed, by a whole 4.2%, much surpassing the 0.6% rebound a month ago. Economists had forecast a 0.5% increase.

Exports to EU countries grew by 3.5% compared to August, and imports from these countries rose by 4.9%.

On a yearly basis, growth in exports climbed to 7.6% from 7% in August.

Annual growth in imports also jumped to 8.7% from 6.4%. Exports to the United States were 10.3% higher, data showed.

The executive committee of the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), the junior partner in Germany's conservative-led coalition government, supports the nomination of Bavarian parliamentary speaker Ilse Aigner as next German president, according to the AFP news agency, citing party sources.

Aigner is "an experienced, down-to-earth politician and possesses the important ability to bring together people over party and social boundaries," according to the quoted sources.

Aigner, 61, who is a member of the center-right Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU), already has the support of both her party and the CDU.

Members of other parties, such as the Green Party, have also said they are in favor of Aigner, who, if elected in a vote by the Federal Convention on January 30, would become Germany's first female head of state and the first CSU member in the position.

People across Germany are remembering the events of November 9, 1989, when the Berlin Wall separating the part of the city in former communist East Germany from that in West Germany was breached, paving the way to German reunification in 1990.

One main ceremony of commemoration is to be held at the Berlin Wall Memorial in the German capital.

President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is also to meet with former East German civil rights activists in the Goethe House in Weimar, the birthplace and childhood home of famous German writer Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.

In the eastern city of Cottbus, the premier of the state of Brandenburg, Dietmar Woidke, is also to host a ceremony in remembrance of the events 37 years ago.

The Berlin Wall encircled West Berlin for 28 years, separating it from East Berlin and surrounding East Germany, known as the German Democratic Republic (DDR).

Its main purpose was to prevent East Germans from escaping from their repressive country to the West, though authorities in the Soviet Bloc cast it as a defense against "fascism" coming from outside.

The trial of eight people suspected of belonging to a militant neo-Nazi group, the "Saxon Separatists," continues in Dresden on Monday.

The men are accused, among other things, of "preparing a traitorous endeavor" as part of their involvement with a terrorist organization.

Prosecutors believe the group, which uses the abbreviation "SS" — like that used by the paramilitary "Schutzstaffel" that operated in the Nazi era — planned to overthrow democracy in Germany, starting with an armed takeover of the eastern state of Saxony.

The eight men  were arrested in November 2024 during international raids conducted in Germany, Austria and Poland and have been remanded in custody since then.

The trial, which began in January, is scheduled to last until December

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has used the November 9 anniversary of several important dates in German history to call on people in Germany and Europe to stand up for democracy and liberty.

November 9 was the day in 1918 that the monarchy fell, in 1938 a day of antisemitic violence known as the November pogroms, and in 1989 the day when the Berlin Wall opened, paving the way for the reunification of Germany.

Writing on X, Merz said, "November 9 stands for the darkest and the happiest hours of our history: for antisemitism and persecution, for the beginning of democracy and the fall of the Wall."

"Freedom and democracy can never be taken for granted. Let us defend them — in Germany and Europe," he wrote.

Commemorations are to be held nationwide to commemorate the Nazi pogroms of November 9-10, 1938, when mobs went on an antisemitic rampage, killing at least 91 Jewish people, ransacking Jewish businesses and burning down hundreds of synagogues.

President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is to attend events in the eastern city of Weimar, where he is due to lay a wreath and hold a speech at the memorial site established at the site of the former Nazi concentration camp of Buchenwald.

The Jüdische Gemeinde zu Berlin is to have all the names of Jewish Nazi victims read out over the day in commemoration of the pogroms.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz will be attending a ceremony marking the 20th anniversary of the Ohel Jakob Main Synagogue in Munich, which was opened 68 years to the day after the main synagogue in the city was destroyed in the pogroms.

The pogroms are sometimes known as "Reichskristallnacht" or "Night of Broken Glass," but this name has fallen out of favor as underplaying the horrors of what happened.

#311. Peacock is redesigning its mobile app to focus more on vertical videos

This is an attempt to “win another hour per user, per month.”

NBCUniversal is completely overhauling the Peacock app on mobile. This redesign will further emphasize vertical video content, just like TikTok, YouTube Shorts and all the rest. Company chairman Matt Strauss recently said that this is an attempt to "win another hour per user, per month," according to The Hollywood Reporter.

"We recognize that we have to start thinking of ourselves less as a streaming platform and more of an entertainment platform," Strauss said. "How do we super serve our franchises and our fandoms where the best experience is on our app?"

Bravo fandom has always extended far beyond the episode itself. @Inc goes inside how @Peacock is building on that passion with Your Bravoverse, a new personalized experience that helps fans explore two decades of unforgettable @BravoTV moments. https://t.co/PETJdEzTsy

— NBCUniversal (@NBCUniversal) November 4, 2026

In addition to a larger emphasis on vertical video, the app is launching fandom hubs for various franchises, like the Bravo-verse or The Office. These hubs will be home to short videos and affiliated experiences. For instance, the Law & Order page will feature little video games to fool around with. The NBA page will offer "easy access to player stats" and "deeper game information sitting directly underneath the live feed in a dual screen view."

There are a couple of techy features heading to the app. Peacock will continue to experiment with live vertical video. There will soon be a "dynamic video player" that automatically switches between vertical and horizontal orientations depending on the device. Of course, the app is also integrating generative AI to allow for "conversational AI search."

🚨BREAKING FROM #BRAVOFANFEST🚨 Allow us to set the scene... Craig Conover stars in an all-new original scripted microdrama, Charmed by a Southern Monster! Stream November 9th on the @Peacock mobile app. #SouthernCharm pic.twitter.com/QpzjT0YE2X

Finally, NBCUniversal intends to continue investing in microdramas. These are extremely short (often just a minute long) serial dramas that connect to tell a larger story. The platform recently released something called Charmed by a Southern Monster, which is the company's first scripted microdrama. The new Peacock app is rolling out now via a phased release that could take until next year to reach every user.

It's worth noting that Peacock recently became profitable for the first time ever. As a matter of fact, it has experienced two straight quarters of profit. We'll have to wait and see if this app redesign helps to continue this trend.

#310. Turkey Promotes Itself as a Climate Champion. Not Everyone Agrees.

Critics say some of the country’s environmental policies run counter to the image it is offering as host of a United Nations climate summit.

Turkey’s global ambitions are written all over the walls of the sprawling conference center in Antalya, the Mediterranean resort city where it is host to the United Nations climate summit that opened on Monday.

“Turkey, where dialogue becomes action,” read giant signs throughout the venue.

“The Future of the World is in Turkey!” read others.

President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has long sought to position Turkey as a rising economic and military power that can mediate conflicts and play a muscular role in international affairs. Welcoming the tens of thousands of officials, ecologists, activists and others attending the U.N. summit, known as COP31, gives the country an opportunity to extend its diplomatic efforts into the critical realm of climate diplomacy, experts said.

But Turkey’s efforts to portray itself as a climate champion run counter to some of its policies, critics said, and to its suppression of environmental activism. They say the country lacks a clear timeline for phasing out coal, continues to import large amounts of plastic waste from Europe and is heavy-handed in its treatment of residents who oppose mining projects.

The climate summit comes months after Turkey hosted its fellow members of the NATO military alliance in the Turkish capital, Ankara, where it showcased its value as a defense partner in an unstable region and the bonhomie between Mr. Erdogan and President Trump.

Now, Turkey seeks to cast itself as a key player in international climate talks, too.

“Turkey wants to show itself as a global power in many different places, including for peace, for climate, for trade,” said Umit Sahin, who heads the climate change program at Istanbul Policy Center, a research institute.

#309. Big Walk used AI to fix a bug. Now the indie gaming world is having a reckoning.

Any amount of AI coding is too much for many Independent Games Festival judges.

The last few years have seen significant debate over the widespread use of AI-powered tools in game development and the responsible disclosure of that usage to players. That debate has exploded into a full-blown controversy in the indie game development space this week, as Big Walk developer House House has publicly and belatedly disclosed minimal AI use in its popular co-operative puzzle exploration game.

This particular controversy has been brewing behind the scenes for months, as judges and jury members for the prestigious Independent Games Festival Awards discussed the issue in private discussion groups. But the debate started to break into public view on Monday when 19 members of the 50-plus-member jury released a signed statement outlining a stance “declining to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity.”

Noting “a significant increase in the number of submitted games developer with generative AI tools,” the group of jurors called out AI’s ecological, economic, psychological, and labor harms in rejecting tools whose use, they said, is still “not a foregone conclusion in our industry.”

The jurors also urged the IGF as a whole to “adopt a strong anti-AI policy for future years that disallows games containing any AI-generated work.”

Although the jurors’ statement didn’t name any specific games, by Tuesday morning, one critical darling in particular was increasingly being noted as a central part of the debate. In a statement provided to Aftermath (and added to the game’s FAQ page shortly thereafter), developer House House admitted publicly that “LLMs were used sparingly” near the end of Big Walk‘s development “to help work through some difficult technical challenges and bugs.”

That limited AI use—which House House says represents “well under 0.1% of Big Walk‘s code—stemmed in part from a thorny Unity engine bug that was slowing the game down with “infinite length” shadows during some game situations. After consulting with a Unity engineer who determined a fix “wasn’t possible,” House House said it consulted an LLM chatbot, which suggested a possible fix that the developers “had to modify… extensively” into the 10 lines of code that ended up in the final game (At least one social media user says the bug was indeed fixable with significant human effort, though).

House House said it didn’t disclose this LLM usage for Big Walk‘s Steam release earlier this year because Valve “does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage.” Indeed, Valve’s AI disclosure form for developers specifically notes that it is concerned with AI-generated content, not “efficiency gains” from “modern game development environments [that] have AI powered tools built into them.”

The IGF Awards make no such distinction for AI usage, however, which led House House to mention its AI-assisted bug fix in submitting the game for awards consideration. A version of that disclosure is being made public now because “it has become a matter of public interest,” House House said.

“This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal,” House House wrote. “We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalization of this technology, or its treatment as ‘inevitable.’ We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologize that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards.”

Learning of House House’s AI disclosure was particularly painful for some IGF judges who had previously felt a special connection to Big Walk. In a blog post discussing his feelings, IGF jurist Austin Walker called the game “an achievement” that was “remarkable” and “beautiful,” featuring puzzles that “capture a range of play that is largely abandoned by the digital form.” Fellow jurist Damon Reece shared in a blog post that the game is “seriously special to me” and that it gave him “a profound and powerful emotional reaction to being in a space that felt like home.”

But when it comes to IGF awards consideration, Walker and Reece were among those who said that even minimal use of AI tools overrode that deep and abiding respect for the work itself.

“We have our hands on the lever here,” Reece wrote. “This is pain that has to happen [emphasis in original] to try and steer our culture away from this. We need to choose to speak loudly and clearly on this, to prioritize human creativity and labour, to tell the culture and the world that this is unacceptable to us. To do otherwise is rank cowardice.”

This isn’t the first time AI usage has noticeably affected game award judging. Last year, the Indie Game Awards (which are completely separate from the IGF Awards) rescinded awards for Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 after the developers admitted that some in-game textures were made using AI tools (these were later patched out).

“The Indie Game Awards have a hard stance on the use of gen AI throughout the nomination process and during the ceremony itself,” they said at the time.

Since House House’s public disclosure, the anti-AI contingent of IGF judges has found plenty of support from disappointed Big Walk fans and industry observers. In the last few days, the game’s Steam page has been bombed with over 400 negative reviews, though Steam’s anti-review-bomb tools seem to be limiting the impact on the game’s overall “Very Positive” reception there.

But others feel House House’s relatively minimal use of AI here is being blown out of proportion. They say it’s important to differentiate between games that use LLMs as a last-resort technical fix, for instance, and others that lean heavily on AI to generate the bulk of their art, music, or the core of the game engine itself.

IGF judge Liz Ryerson wrote on social media that she didn’t find House House’s AI use to be personally disqualifying for the awards and that “the fact that many acted like there aren’t any levels to this and it’s all the same is bothersome to me.”

“To feel like someone gets punished a lot more for transparency about a smaller level of fuckup vs. just not even attempting to be honest or transparent at all is what bothers me,” she wrote.

Steam Hype staff writer and prolific Steam curator Dominic Tarason also pushed back against the idea that “House House need to be memory-holed and their work never spoken of again” as a “penalty for touching the Forbidden Device.” He said he considers Big Walk “very mildly compromised art” that is still “absolutely, unquestionably art and very human.”

“They spent years on that work of art,” Tarason added. “They asked a chatbot for two minutes how to fix a bug. That’s a ‘That’s lame, don’t do that again’ failing. … Some of you are acting like they’ve been convicted of high crimes against humanity, to be sealed away in the darkest oubliette until not even bones remain.”

But some have argued that using AI to fix a bug rather than hiring an expert to figure it out did make the game’s development at least a bit less human than it could have been. “House House aren’t laying off developers to replace them with Claude, and I’m sure they would be firmly against the mere thought of doing this, but we can also clearly see how their actions are part of the same problem,” AI researcher Mike Cook wrote on his blog.

Still, game developer, author, and professor Brendan Keogh wrote that he thinks “an extreme zero tolerance of any [generative AI] is ultimately counterproductive now. [There’s] a lot of anger at devs that feel deeply conflicted enough about their glorified Google search to disclose it, and [that is] encouraging those using it to actually steal labor to hide that use.”

As time goes on and AI tools are increasingly used in the building of major game engines, it may become increasingly difficult for anti-AI absolutists to avoid every game that has been touched by even a hint of LLM-generated code (if that use is even disclosed in the first place). That said, many still see value in a firm and unyielding public stance against what they see as a scourge to their entire industry.

“I think zero tolerance is a viable political position,” narrative designer and writer Hannah Nicklin wrote on social media. “You use politics against systems, for people you affect change through connection and understanding… The IGF jury statement… levels itself at a system of shared value and asks for change to enable solidarity around a position of harm reduction.”

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#308. Who is Ilse Aigner, leading candidate for Germany's next president?

She would be the first female president and the first Christian Social Union politician to hold Germany's highest office. Ilse Aigner is the favored candidate for the Federal Convention vote on January 30.

Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner has emerged as the leading candidate to succeed Frank-Walter Steinmeier as president of Germany, a largely ceremonial office, but who is the head of state and regarded as a moral authority for the nation.

News emerged over the weekend that Chancellor and Christian Democratic Union (CDU) leader Friedrich Merz favored Aigner, a veteran of the CDU's sister-party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), and currently president of the Bavarian parliament.

A specially convened assembly, the Federal Convention, will gather on January 30, 2027, to elect the next German president. Since the CDU, CSU, and their coalition partner the Social Democratic Party (SPD) have a majority in the convention, Aigner's election is considered highly likely.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Aigner is in many respects an unusual politician, especially in Germany, where a law degree often seems to be a prerequisite for a political career. The 61-year-old has no university degree at all, though she did train as a telecommunications technician to join her parents' electrical business.

She spent several years working for the military helicopter company Eurocopter, since bought by the aviation and defense giant Airbus, where she developed electrical components.

Aigner entered the Bavarian parliament for the CSU in 1994 and then served from 1998 to 2013 in Germany's federal parliament, the Bundestag. From 2008 to 2013, she was agriculture and consumer protection minister under then Chancellor Angela Merkel.

Both of these portfolios come with considerable pressure from the public, especially during food scandals, and from powerful lobbying organizations, as well as conflicts at EU level. Aigner navigated this period without any major crises and was generally well regarded.

The personnel policies of political parties can often seem like a game of chess. In 2013, Aigner left national politics and moved back to her home state to serve as Bavaria's economy minister under then State Premier Horst Seehofer, who tried to establish her as his successor.

But then came Markus Söder, at the time Bavaria's finance minister and for a long time Seehofer's biggest rival inside the CSU. It was Söder, a colorful character who also harbored pretensions to be German chancellor, who won out in the power struggle that followed Seehofer's retirement and became Bavarian state premier in 2018.

Aigner and Söder both entered Bavaria's state parliament in 1994, when they were the state's two youngest lawmakers, and their political paths have been intertwined since. Though Söder's rise to power prevented Aigner from becoming state premier, she has served as president of Bavaria's state parliament for the past eight years, and is a highly respected authority figure in the state.

For months now, Aigner has been named as a potential candidate for Germany's head of state after Steinmeier's constitutionally enforced exit next year.

Söder himself openly mentioned her as a suitable candidate back in April, and there have been indications of support from several CDU and CSU representatives, but also from the ranks of the center-left SPD and the environmentalist Greens. But Merz seemed wary for a long time. Other names came — and went.

When the chancellor greeted Aigner by name in his opening remarks to a CSU meeting in Munich in October, he had to pause for thunderous applause from the delegates, who rose to their feet to celebrate the veteran politician.

In January, the Bavarian Merkur newspaper reported on Aigner's visit to a school in the town of Tegernsee, where she answered questions from fourth graders for their student newspaper. The CSU politician told them that she had not planned her career, but she was never able to "keep her mouth shut" and this was also part of why she had been elected to her various offices.

However, it was also noticeable that she was entirely capable of "keeping her mouth shut" when it was judicious to do so: She has largely refrained from commenting publicly during the internal maneuvering for the candidacy within the Union parties.

Aigner would not only be Germany's first female president, but also the first to be single and never married. Though men have dominated the office, there have been female nominees in almost every election since 1999. That year, the Union put forward Thuringian physicist Dagmar Schipanski, while the Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), precursor to the socialist Left Party, put forward theologian Uta Ranke-Heinemann in the race against Social Democrat Johannes Rau.

But considering the majority needed in the Federal Convention, both were effectively just token candidates from minority parties, as have been all the other female candidates since. That's one reason why there has been pressure to finally choose a woman as the majority candidate. Aigner has long enjoyed respect from the conservative camp.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany has never had a president, or indeed a chancellor, from the CSU, a regional party that nevertheless wields national power thanks to its alliance with the CDU. One CSU lawmaker, Richard Stücklen, spent four years as president of the Bundestag — formally the country's second-highest office — from 1979.

If the door to the presidency does open for Aigner, many believe it would shut out Söder's ambitions to become chancellor. The CDU, a much bigger conservative party, usually overrules the CSU when it comes to choosing a chancellor candidate when the general election comes around, and it seems unlikely that the CDU would tolerate two CSU figures leading the country.

But Aigner's election would also remove one of Söder's key rivals back home: Aigner, still only 61, enjoys excellent popularity ratings and is considered a natural rival to the 59-year-old state premier.

Ultimately, by nominating Aigner, Merz is also paving the way for someone from the CDU to become the next chancellor provided the CDU/CSU wins the next federal election, of course.

But first, the Federal Convention must make its decision on January 30. The new German president will officially assume office in mid-March.

This article was originally written in German.
